title: Pelias
titleEn: The Daughters of Pelias — Metamorphoses VII.297–349
source: P. Ovidius Naso, Metamorphoses, ed. Hugo Magnus (Gotha: F.A. Perthes), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-latinLit phi0959.phi006.perseus-lat2, sha256 fb3fdb1d8a4a3b82. Collated against The Latin Library (cltk mirror) as a disagreement detector only. Pronunciation convention: reconstructed Classical (restored) Latin.
about: Medea, having boasted of stripping the decay of age from Jason's father, stages a quarrel with her husband and arrives as a suppliant at the door of Pelias, whose daughters take her in because their father is too old to do it himself. She never asks for anything: she lets the girls arrive at the hope themselves, then proves the art by cutting the throat of a worn-out ram, out of whose cauldron a lamb leaps. The second time she sets on the fire only clear water and herbs with no power in them, and the daughters, told that a father's old age can be let out through his wounds, take up their swords over his drugged body. They cannot look while they strike, and Medea finishes what their nerve will not.

sentences.t:
Neve doli cessent, odium cum coniuge falsum
Phasias adsimulat Peliaeque ad limina supplex
confugit.
sentences.l: And lest her guiles fall idle, the Phasian woman feigns a false hatred with her husband and, a suppliant, flees for refuge to the threshold of Pelias.
sentences.i: And so that her cunning should not lie idle, the woman of Phasis pretends to have fallen out with her husband, and takes refuge as a suppliant at the door of Pelias.
sentences.n: Phasias is “the woman of the Phasis”, the river of Colchis: this is Medea, who is never called by her name in this part but only Phasias, Colchis, Aeetias, venefica. Neve doli cessent is a negative purpose clause, “and lest her tricks come to a stop”. Odium falsum cum coniuge is a staged quarrel with Jason, not hatred felt.

sentences.t:
Atque illam, quoniam gravis ipse senecta est,
excipiunt natae.
sentences.l: And her, since he himself is heavy with old age, his daughters receive.
sentences.i: And since Pelias himself is weighed down by old age, it is his daughters who take her in.
sentences.n: Ipse points to Pelias, not to Medea: he is too burdened by years to receive a suppliant himself, so the daughters do it. Senecta is ablative with gravis, “heavy with old age”. The word order puts illam, the suppliant, first and the daughters last, where the sentence turns.

sentences.t:
Quas tempore callida parvo
Colchis amicitiae mendacis imagine cepit.
sentences.l: And these, in a short space of time, the cunning Colchian woman took with the show of a lying friendship.
sentences.i: And in a short while the cunning Colchian had them, with a show of counterfeit friendship.
sentences.n: Quas is a connecting relative — a relative pronoun opening a new sentence where English would start afresh: “and them”. It comes twice more in this part, as cuius and quem. Cepit is the verb of catching and taking in, not of physical seizure. Colchis here is the noun “the Colchian woman”, another name-by-country for Medea.

sentences.t:
Dumque refert inter meritorum maxima, demptos
Aesonis esse situs, atque hac in parte moratur,
spes est virginibus Pelia subiecta creatis
arte suum parili revirescere posse parentem.
sentences.l: And while she recounts, among the greatest of her services, that Aeson's mouldering has been taken away, and lingers on this part, a hope is slipped beneath the maidens born of Pelias that their own parent can grow green again by a like art.
sentences.i: And while she counts among her greatest kindnesses the stripping of decay from Aeson, and dwells on that point, a hope is worked into the daughters of Pelias that a like art could make their own father green again.
sentences.n: Situs is the mould and stiffness that settles on an old body; demptos esse situs is an indirect statement after refert, “that the decay had been taken away”. Aeson is Jason's father, whom Medea claims to have renewed. Spes est subiecta is passive with the hope as its subject, “a hope is slipped under them”: Medea proposes nothing, she lets the idea rise in them. Pelia creatis is the ablative of origin, “born from Pelias”. Revirescere is “to turn green again”, the metaphor of a tree.

sentences.t: Idque petunt pretiumque iubent sine fine pacisci.
sentences.l: And this they seek, and they bid her strike a bargain for a price without end.
sentences.i: This they beg for, and tell her to name her price, with no limit set.
sentences.n: Pacisci is a deponent, passive in form and active in sense: “to strike a bargain”. Sine fine is “without limit” rather than “for ever” — they will pay whatever she asks.

sentences.t:
Illa brevi spatio silet et dubitare videtur
suspenditque animos ficta gravitate rogantes.
sentences.l: She for a short space is silent and seems to hesitate, and holds their asking hearts in suspense with a feigned gravity.
sentences.i: For a little while she says nothing and seems to waver, and with a counterfeit solemnity keeps their pleading hearts hanging.
sentences.n: Rogantes is a participle agreeing with animos: the hearts themselves do the asking, “the pleading hearts”. Magnus prints rogantes; some editions print rogantum, “of those asking”, which puts the participle on the daughters instead, with the same effect. Suspendit is the physical verb “hangs up”, used of holding someone in suspense. Ficta gravitate is ablative of manner: the gravity is manufactured.

sentences.t:
Mox ubi pollicita est, “quo sit fiducia maior
muneris huius” ait, “qui vestri maximus aevo est
dux gregis inter oves, agnus medicamine fiet.”
sentences.l: Soon, when she had promised, “so that confidence in this gift may be greater,” she says, “he who is greatest in age among the sheep, the leader of your flock, shall become a lamb by a drug.”
sentences.i: Then, once she had given her promise: “So that you may trust this gift the more,” she says, “the oldest of the sheep, the ram that leads your flock, shall be turned into a lamb by my medicine.”
sentences.n: Pollicita est is deponent, passive in form and active in sense: “she promised”. Quo with a comparative (maior) is the standard way of introducing a purpose clause that contains a comparison: “so that the confidence may be the greater”. Maximus aevo is “greatest in respect of age”, an ablative of respect. Vestri goes with gregis, not with oves: the flock is theirs, and dux gregis is the bellwether that walks in front. Medicamen covers drug, potion and charm at once.

sentences.t:
Protinus innumeris effetus laniger annis
attrahitur flexo circum cava tempora cornu.
sentences.l: At once the wool-bearer, worn out by countless years, is dragged forward by the horn curved around his hollow temples.
sentences.i: At once the ram, spent with years past counting, is hauled in by the horn that curls around his sunken temples.
sentences.n: Laniger, “wool-bearer”, is a compound standing in for the plain word ram. Flexo cornu is ablative of means: they lead him by the horn, which curves back around his head. Cava tempora, “hollow temples”, is the sunkenness of extreme age.

sentences.t:
Cuius ut Haemonio marcentia guttura cultro
fodit et exiguo maculavit sanguine ferrum,
membra simul pecudis validosque venefica sucos
mergit in aere cavo:
sentences.l: And when she had pierced his withering throat with a Haemonian knife and had stained the iron with scanty blood, the poison-woman plunges at the same time the beast's limbs and her strong juices into the hollow bronze:
sentences.i: And the moment she had driven the Thessalian blade into his sagging throat and stained the iron with what little blood there was, the poisoner plunged the creature's limbs and her potent juices together into the hollow bronze:
sentences.n: Cuius is the connecting relative again, in the genitive: “and his”, holding the ram over from the last sentence. Haemonio is “Thessalian” — Haemonia is the old name of Thessaly, the country of witchcraft. Exiguo sanguine is the point of the line: a beast that old has little blood left to spill. Venefica is the noun Ovid gives Medea here, “the poison-woman”, and aere names the cauldron by its metal, bronze.

sentences.t:
minuunt en corporis artus
cornuaque exurunt nec non cum cornibus annos,
et tener auditur medio balatus aeno.
sentences.l: look, they lessen the limbs of his body and burn away the horns, and with the horns the years as well, and a tender bleating is heard in the middle of the bronze.
sentences.i: look — they shrink the limbs of his body, burn the horns away, and the years along with the horns, and a thin bleating is heard from the middle of the cauldron.
sentences.n: En is the poet's “look”, turning the reader into a spectator at the cauldron; Magnus prints en, while some editions print ea, “those things”, which supplies an explicit subject for the verbs instead of leaving it understood. The subject of minuunt and exurunt is the juices either way. Nec non is a double negative used for emphatic addition, “and what is more”. Cum cornibus annos: the years burn off along with the horns, which are where an old ram's age shows.

sentences.t:
Nec mora, balatum mirantibus exsilit agnus
lascivitque fuga lactantiaque ubera quaerit.
sentences.l: No delay: as they marvel at the bleating, a lamb leaps out and frisks away in flight and looks for milk-filled udders.
sentences.i: In an instant, while they are still wondering at the bleat, a lamb springs out, skips off at a run, and goes looking for a milky udder.
sentences.n: Mirantibus is a dative participle with its own object balatum, “for them, as they marvel at the bleating”: the daughters are the people it happens in front of. Nec mora, “and no delay”, is a stock phrase for an instant change. Lascivit fuga is “it plays with running”, the skipping of a newborn, and lactantia ubera are udders in milk: the lamb goes looking to suckle.

sentences.t:
Obstipuere satae Pelia: promissaque postquam
exhibuere fidem, tum vero impensius instant.
sentences.l: The daughters sown from Pelias were struck dumb; and after the promises had shown their good faith, then indeed they press the more insistently.
sentences.i: The daughters of Pelias stood astonished; and once the promise had made good its word, then they pressed her all the harder.
sentences.n: Obstipuere and exhibuere are the poetic third-plural perfect in -ere for -erunt (obstipuerunt, exhibuerunt) — the metre invites it, and you will meet the form again in this part. Satae Pelia is the ablative of origin once more, “sown from Pelias”. Promissa exhibuere fidem has the promises as subject: “the promises produced their credit”, that is, they came true. Instant is the verb of pressing hard on someone.

sentences.t:
Ter iuga Phoebus equis in Hibero flumine mersis
dempserat et quarta radiantia nocte micabant
sidera, cum rapido fallax Aeetias igni
imponit purum laticem et sine viribus herbas.
sentences.l: Three times Phoebus had taken the yokes from his horses, plunged in the Iberian river, and on the fourth night the radiant stars were shining, when the deceiving daughter of Aeetes sets on a swift fire clear water and herbs without powers.
sentences.i: Three times the Sun had unyoked his horses in the western river, and on the fourth night the stars were blazing, when the treacherous daughter of Aeetes set clear water and powerless herbs over a racing fire.
sentences.n: Equis is best taken as dative with dempserat, “took the yokes off his horses”, with mersis agreeing with equis; because dative and ablative are identical here, the same two words can also be read as an ablative absolute, “with his horses plunged in the river”. The Iberian river is the water of the far west, where the sun goes down; three unyokings and a fourth night is Ovid's way of counting the days out. Aeetias is “the daughter of Aeetes”, Medea named by her father this time. Purum laticem et sine viribus herbas is the whole trick stated in advance: plain water and herbs with no power in them.

sentences.t:
Iamque neci similis resoluto corpore regem
et cum rege suo custodes somnus habebat,
quem dederant cantus magicaeque potentia linguae:
sentences.l: And now a sleep like death, with the body unstrung, was holding the king, and along with their king the guards — a sleep which incantations and the power of a magic tongue had given.
sentences.i: And by now a sleep like death held the king with his limbs gone loose, and the guards along with their king — a sleep given him by spells and the power of an enchanting tongue.
sentences.n: Resoluto corpore is a genuine ablative absolute, “with his body unstrung”: the noun is not governed by anything else in the sentence. Neci similis is dative with similis, “like to death”. Quem is the connecting relative picking up somnus, “and this sleep”. Somnus is the subject holding both regem and custodes, so the guarding fails at the same moment the king does.

sentences.t:
intrarant iussae cum Colchide limina natae
ambierantque torum.
sentences.l: The daughters, bidden, had entered the doorway with the Colchian woman and had gone around the bed.
sentences.i: The daughters had come in through the door with the Colchian, as they were told, and had ringed the bed.
sentences.n: Intrarant is the shortened form of intraverant, “they had entered”; poets drop the -ve- of the perfect stem freely. Iussae is a perfect passive participle agreeing with natae, “having been ordered”: they are already acting under instruction. Ambierant, from ambio, is “they had gone around” — they are standing in a ring about the bed before she speaks.

sentences.t:
“Quid nunc dubitatis inertes?
Stringite” ait “gladios veteremque haurite cruorem,
ut repleam vacuas iuvenali sanguine venas.
sentences.l: “Why do you hesitate now, you do-nothings? Draw,” she says, “your swords, and drain out the old gore, so that I may fill the emptied veins with young blood.
sentences.i: “Why hang back now, you useless things? Draw your swords,” she says, “and let the old gore out, so that I can fill the emptied veins with young blood.
sentences.n: Inertes is Medea's word for them, “without skill, without spirit”, and it is contempt spoken to their faces; the English keeps it at that strength. Cruor is not the blood in the body but blood spilled, gore — she uses cruor for what is to come out and sanguis for what she says will go in. Haurite is “draw out, drain”, the verb of drawing water from a well.

sentences.t:
In manibus vestris vita est aetasque parentis:
si pietas ulla est nec spes agitatis inanes,
officium praestate patri telisque senectam
exigite et saniem coniecto emittite ferro.”
sentences.l: In your hands is the life and the age of your parent. If there is any devotion, and you are not turning over empty hopes, render your duty to your father, and with your weapons drive out his old age and let the corrupt blood out with the iron thrust in.”
sentences.i: Your father's life and his years are in your hands. If you have any family duty in you, and are not nursing hopes that come to nothing, do your father this service: drive his old age out with your blades, and let the tainted blood run with a thrust of the steel.”
sentences.n: Pietas is the duty owed to a parent, and Medea makes it the argument for stabbing him. Agitatis is second person plural, “you turn over, you nurse”, with spes inanes as its object. Senectam exigite uses exigo in its medical sense, “drive out” a disease: the old age is to be let out through the wounds. Sanies is diseased, corrupted blood, set against the iuvenalis sanguis she promises. Coniecto ferro is an ablative of means with a participle on it, “with the iron driven in” — the iron is the instrument of emittite, not a separate absolute clause.

sentences.t:
His, ut quaeque pia est, hortatibus impia prima est,
et ne sit scelerata, facit scelus.
sentences.l: At these urgings, each, in the measure that she is dutiful, is first in being undutiful; and so that she may not be wicked, she does a wickedness.
sentences.i: At her urging, the more loving a daughter is, the quicker she is to do the unnatural thing; and to keep from being a criminal, each commits a crime.
sentences.n: Pia and impia are the same word turned inside out: pietas is the duty owed to a parent, so the daughter who loves her father most is the first to strike him. Ut quaeque pia est is the correlative “in proportion as each one is”. Ne sit scelerata, facit scelus repeats the trick in the sound of the words: to avoid being a criminal she commits the crime. His hortatibus is ablative, “at these urgings”, and the two halves of it are split apart around the paradox.

sentences.t:
Haud tamen ictus
ulla suos spectare potest, oculosque reflectunt
caecaque dant saevis aversae vulnera dextris.
sentences.l: Yet not one of them can look at her own blows, and they turn their eyes away, and, turned away, they deal blind wounds with savage right hands.
sentences.i: Yet none of them can watch her own stroke; they turn their eyes aside, and with their faces averted they deal blind wounds with cruel hands.
sentences.n: Caeca vulnera are “blind wounds” in the active sense — struck by someone who is not looking, not wounds that blind. Aversae is a participle agreeing with the daughters, “turned away”. The line is arranged so that the savagery sits in the hands (saevis dextris) while the faces are elsewhere. Ulla is the indefinite “any one of them” after the negative haud.

sentences.t:
Ille, cruore fluens, cubito tamen adlevat artus
semilacerque toro temptat consurgere et inter
tot medius gladios pallentia bracchia tendens
“quid facitis, gnatae? quis vos in fata parentis
armat?” ait.
sentences.l: He, running with gore, still lifts his limbs on his elbow and, half torn apart, tries to rise from the couch, and in the middle of so many swords, stretching out his pallid arms, says “What are you doing, my daughters? Who arms you for your father's death?”
sentences.i: He, streaming with gore, still props his body up on an elbow and, half torn to pieces, tries to rise from the bed; and there in the middle of all those blades, holding out his whitening arms, he says: “What are you doing, my daughters? Who arms you against your father's life?”
sentences.n: Semilacer, “half torn”, is a rare compound: semi-, “half”, welded to lacer, “torn”. Medius inter tot gladios is literal placement: he is the centre of the ring of swords. In fata parentis is “for the death of your father”, fata being the appointed end. Gnatae is the older form of natae, “daughters”, and the word is itself the appeal — he names the relation while they are cutting him. Magnus prints quis, “who arms you”; some editions print quid, “what arms you”, which asks after a cause rather than a person.

sentences.t: Cecidere illis animique manusque.
sentences.l: Their spirits and their hands fell from them.
sentences.i: Their courage failed them, and their hands dropped.
sentences.n: Cecidere is the poetic perfect in -ere again (ceciderunt). Illis is a dative of the person concerned: the spirits and the hands are theirs, and it is on them that the loss falls. One verb serves both subjects, and the two -que endings tie them together: the nerve and the hands go down in the same instant.

sentences.t:
Plura locuturo cum verbis guttura Colchis
abstulit et calidis laniatum mersit in undis.
sentences.l: From him about to say more the Colchian woman took away his throat together with his words, and plunged him, mangled, in the hot water.
sentences.i: He would have said more; the Colchian took his throat away along with the words, and sank his mangled body in the scalding water.
sentences.n: Locuturo is a future participle in the dative, “from him about to say more”: the sentence cuts him off at the same place the knife does. Cum verbis guttura abstulit takes the words and the windpipe in one phrase, since the throat is what was making the words. Laniatum, “mangled”, is a participle standing in for the man himself. The hot water is the cauldron she set on the fire, the one holding plain water and powerless herbs.
